related_questions.question: How long will I live with HER2-positive breast cancer?
related_questions.snippet: Providers may consider someone to be cured if that person was alive five years after receiving a diagnosis of HER2-positive breast cancer. According to data kept by the U.S. National Cancer Institute (NCI), more than 90% of people were alive five years after receiving their diagnosis.

related_questions.question: Is HER2-positive breast cancer good or bad?
related_questions.snippet: Breast cancer identified as HER2-positive tends to grow faster, spread (metastatic breast cancer) and come back (recur). While HER2-positive cancer may be aggressive, it also responds better to breast cancer treatment that targets HER2 proteins.
related_questions.title: HER2 Positive Breast Cancer - Penn Medicine

related_questions.question: Can you have HER2-positive breast cancer without chemotherapy?

text_blocks.snippet: While chemotherapy is often a standard part of treatment for HER2-positive breast cancer, it may be possible to avoid or minimize it in some cases, particularly for early-stage disease with specific characteristics. Factors like tumor size, lymph node involvement, hormone receptor status, and individual patient characteristics influence the decision, and newer studies are exploring chemotherapy-sparing approaches with targeted therapies.

list.title: Tumor size and lymph node status:
list.snippet: Smaller tumors (especially those 1 cm or less) and those without lymph node involvement may be candidates for less intensive treatment, including the potential to omit chemotherapy.

list.title: Hormone receptor status:
list.snippet: HER2-positive breast cancers that are also hormone receptor-positive (meaning they are fueled by estrogen or progesterone) may be more amenable to chemotherapy de-escalation, as hormone therapy can play a significant role in treatment.

list.title: Age and overall health:
list.snippet: Older patients or those with other health conditions may be considered for chemotherapy avoidance if their prognosis without it is still favorable, according to the Breast Cancer.org.

list.title: Response to initial treatment:
list.snippet: Some trials are exploring a "treat-and-de-escalate" approach, where patients initially receive a combination of chemotherapy and HER2-targeted therapy, and if they achieve a good response, chemotherapy may be discontinued.

list.title: Molecular testing:
list.snippet: Tests like Oncotype DX can analyze the genetic makeup of the tumor to help predict the likelihood of recurrence and guide treatment decisions, potentially identifying patients who can safely forgo chemotherapy, according to Healthline.

list.title: HER2-targeted therapy alone:
list.snippet: Some studies have investigated the use of HER2-targeted drugs like trastuzumab (Herceptin) and pertuzumab (Perjeta) with or without other targeted therapies, potentially eliminating or reducing the need for chemotherapy, according to the www.cancertodaymag.org.

list.title: De-escalation trials:
list.snippet: Clinical trials like PHERGain are evaluating whether some patients can safely undergo HER2-targeted therapy without initial chemotherapy, or if chemotherapy can be stopped based on their response to treatment.

list.title: Not all HER2-positive cancers are the same:
list.snippet: There's a wide range of HER2-positive breast cancers, and the need for chemotherapy is individualized.

list.title: Individualized approach:
list.snippet: A multidisciplinary team, including surgeons, medical oncologists, and radiation oncologists, will carefully evaluate each patient's case to determine the most appropriate treatment plan.

list.title: Ongoing research:
list.snippet: Clinical trials continue to explore new ways to personalize treatment for HER2-positive breast cancer, potentially expanding the options for chemotherapy-sparing approaches, according to www.bcm.edu.
